resources.string: This inward fold of the luminal membrane enlarges the surface for acid secretion.
Numerous mitochondria help meet the energy demand of ion transport.
These granules store pepsinogen, a precursor released into the gastric gland lumen.
Protein synthesis takes place on membrane-bound ribosomes in the basal region.
Paneth cells store products such as lysozyme in granules directed toward the intestinal crypt lumen.
The nucleus sits away from the granule-rich surface.
This open-type example reaches the lumen. Some enteroendocrine cells do not contact it.
A basal region releases signals toward nearby tissue and blood, rather than into the gut lumen.
The highlighted teaching example lies among crypt-base epithelial neighbors.
Small-intestinal stem cells can sit between Paneth cells at the crypt base.
The apical primary cilium projects into the bile duct lumen and senses aspects of the local environment.
Transport at the bile-facing surface helps modify ductal fluid.
The enzyme-rich region faces the acinar lumen. Some enzymes are secreted as inactive precursors.
Acinar cells deliver enzymes and precursors into this lumen before they enter the ducts.
The surface facing the duct lumen participates in bicarbonate secretion into pancreatic juice.
The opposite side exchanges solutes with the local tissue; the ducts do not make insulin.
A serous acinar example is shown. Salivary glands can also contain mucous secretory units.
The small lumen receives primary secretion. Downstream ducts modify it.
These granules store glucagon. When released, glucagon can signal the liver to increase glucose output.
Islet hormones can enter the circulation here. The capillary and the pancreatic duct are separate routes.
Some delta cells have processes that extend toward other islet cells.
Somatostatin can modulate nearby insulin and glucagon secretion.
PP (gamma) cells release pancreatic polypeptide, distinct from insulin and glucagon.
As an endocrine cell, it releases hormone toward the surrounding tissue and vessels rather than into a digestive duct.
In this mammary example, myoepithelial processes wrap around the secretory unit and can help move existing milk toward a duct.
The cell sits outside the secretory epithelium, not on the luminal side.
Islet secretions enter local capillaries. The colors identify selected cell examples, not proportions or a ring-shaped arrangement.
Cell identity schematic, not a staining pattern
Acini and islets have different destinations
Acini release digestive enzymes and precursors
Ducts add bicarbonate and drain into the duodenum
Islets release hormones toward the bloodstream
These routes can operate at the same time. The steps compare their destinations, not the timing or amounts of secretion.
The four stages compare cell roles, not a timed release sequence. The illustration does not imply fixed cell proportions.
Mixed concentration = total bicarbonate delivered per minute ÷ combined fluid flow.
The base stream is fixed at 1 mL/min and 20 mmol/L. Both inputs are synthetic. This model only mixes two streams and does not predict pH, acid neutralization, or pancreatic function.
